title: Conformity Under Context
summary: Change six things about a group judgement task and watch conformity split into a normative route and an informational one. Then open the headline percentage into the people behind it.
learningObjectives: Distinguish informational from normative influence by the manipulations that move each of them.
Explain why breaking unanimity matters far more than the size of the majority.
Say what group identification adds that the classic two-route account does not contain.
Read a headline conformity percentage as a summary of a distribution rather than a property of people.
Explain why classic laboratory rates are not constants and why the variation between replications is the finding.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; no task is administered to the person using the tool, and every calculation runs in the browser tab.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, selects, radios and buttons; no dragging and no timing, and the simulated task is never presented to the learner. Each experiment exposes only its own controls and its own result, and the pinned primary is 125px so it stays in view while the six controls are scrolled. The two-route bar chart prints each route's percentage beside its bar and is followed by a sentence naming both values; the histogram prints each bar's count above it and is paired with a visible table. Every range carries an aria-valuetext in words naming both ends of its scale. Focus moves to the new experiment heading when a stage button is pressed. Changes are announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths. Two situational controls are on show - how many others break with the majority, and whether the answer is public - with the other four behind a disclosure. Three of the six classic conditions are on show and three sit beside the controls they move. Controls held back sit inside native <details> elements, reachable by keyboard in one step and announced as collapsed rather than being disabled.
readmeTopic: Two routes to agreement, six things about the situation, and the distribution hiding inside a conformity percentage
simulationNotes: No historical study is reproduced: not its stimuli, not its procedure, not its data. The presets carry recognisable names so the comparison is legible and their outputs are not those results. Conformity on a critical round is modelled as two independent routes - normative = 0.68 x unanimity x audience x identification x norm clarity, informational = 0.75 x ambiguity x (0.4 + 0.6 x majority standing) x unanimity - combined as 1 - (1 - n)(1 - i). Audience appears only in the normative term, which is what makes the private-response manipulation diagnostic. Unanimity is a step function (1.00, 0.30, 0.22, 0.18 normative; 1.00, 0.60, 0.50, 0.45 informational) rather than a proportion, because a single dissenter matters far more than the headcount. With these parameters the six presets give 35, 12, 14, 66, 7 and 67 per cent. Experiment 2 draws 100 simulated participants from mulberry32 with seed 20260311; susceptibility multipliers are drawn once, normalised to a mean of exactly one so the group average reproduces the headline rate, and rounds are Bernoulli draws from a fixed grid. In the classic condition at twelve rounds, 13 of the 100 never conform at all. The parameters are chosen to put the classic conditions in roughly the right order of magnitude, which is a teaching decision and not a replication.
